claims.text: The initial alloy is a single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloy in which Ti and Ni are primary constituents.
The initial alloy can be produced by high-temperature melting followed by homogenization and solution treatment.
Aging the solution-treated alloy at 600°C for 4 hours can induce nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti-type precipitates.
The aging treatment will produce a uniform dispersion of the nanoscale precipitates within the matrix.
The Ni3Ti-type precipitates will remain coherent with the matrix.
The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
The precipitates impede dislocation glide and climb.
Impeded dislocation motion provides precipitation strengthening at elevated temperature.
The aging treatment will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the as-solutionized alloy.
The aging treatment will reduce the elevated-temperature creep rate relative to the as-solutionized alloy.
The aging treatment will improve creep resistance by impeding dislocation glide and climb.
The predicted benefit applies during tensile or creep testing at 700–800°C.
A strain rate of approximately 10^-4 s^-1 is an applicable elevated-temperature tensile-test condition for evaluating the intervention.
The comparison baseline is the same solution-treated alloy without post-solution aging.
Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy systems are less thoroughly explored at elevated temperatures.
A statistically significant yield-strength improvement of at least approximately 10% is proposed as an example success threshold.
Failure to observe the expected nanoscale precipitates would falsify the intervention hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mechanical improvement over the unaged control would falsify the intervention hypothesis.
